passages.t: The Philistines ask how to send it home
passages.happening:
The ark has been in Philistine land for seven months. The Philistines call their priests and diviners: “What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us how to send it back to its place” (verse 2).

The answer is to send it back with a guilt offering, not empty: ‘Then you will be healed, and you will understand why His hand has not been lifted from you’ (verse 3). The offering is to be ‘Five gold tumors and five gold rats’ (verse 4), one for each of the five Philistine rulers. ‘Give glory to the God of Israel, and perhaps He will lift His hand from you and your gods and your land’ (verse 5).

The priests remember Egypt. “Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs?” (verse 6).

Then they set a test. Two cows that are nursing and have never been yoked are to pull a new cart with the ark on it, while their calves are penned up at home. If the cows go up the road toward Beth-shemesh, it was the LORD who sent the disaster. If not, ‘then we will know that it was not His hand that punished us and that it happened by chance’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The Philistines ask their own experts how to appease a foreign god, and the answer follows the practice of their world. A guilt offering paid a god back for an offense. The gold models of tumors and rats hand the affliction itself over to the god who sent it. The five images match the five cities, so each pays its share.

The word for guilt offering is the word Israel's law uses for an offering that makes up for a wrong done against God's holy things. Even outsiders recognize that they owe the LORD something.

Their reference to Pharaoh shows how widely the story of the exodus was known. These priests have learned from history better than the Egyptians did. They tell their people not to harden their hearts, and to give glory to Israel's God.

The test is clever. Nursing cows that had never been yoked would not pull a cart in a straight line on their own, and cows taken from their calves would want to turn back to them. If they walked steadily away from their calves toward Israel, only the LORD could be driving them. The priests want to know whether their suffering was God's hand or chance.

There is a touch of comedy in the first half of the chapter. The great Philistine lords agonize over every detail, and in a moment they will be following two cows to the border.
passages.later:
Joshua used the same words to Achan when he called him to confess: “My son, give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make a confession to Him” (Joshua 7:19).

The plagues of Egypt stand behind the priests' warning. After the last of them Pharaoh finally said, “Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites!” (Exodus 12:31).
passages.asks: The Philistine priests warned their people not to harden their hearts as Pharaoh did. Ask where you have seen what happens when someone refuses to change, and whether you have learned from it. And ask whether you are willing to let God answer a question you put to him, even if the answer is plain.

passages.happening:
The Philistines do as they were told. They hitch the two cows to the cart, pen up the calves, and put the ark on the cart with the chest of gold objects (verses 10-11).

“And the cows headed straight up the road toward Beth-shemesh, staying on that one highway and lowing as they went, never straying to the right or to the left” (verse 12). The Philistine rulers follow them to the border.

The people of Beth-shemesh are harvesting wheat in the valley. ‘When they looked up and saw the ark, they were overjoyed at the sight’ (verse 13). The cart stops in the field of a man named Joshua, by a large rock. The people break up the cart for wood and offer the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD (verse 14). The Levites lift down the ark and the gold, and set them on the rock (verse 15).

The five Philistine rulers watch, and go back to Ekron the same day (verse 16). The gold tumors are one for each city: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Beth-shemesh was an Israelite town on the border with the Philistines, in the Sorek Valley west of Jerusalem. Its name means house of the sun. It had been given to the Levites in Joshua's day, which is why Levites are there to lift down the ark. Excavations at Tel Beth-Shemesh show a border town of the Iron Age, with a way of life different from the nearby Philistine cities.

The wheat harvest in the valley puts the scene in late spring or early summer. The people look up from the harvest and see the ark coming home.

The lowing cows tell the story by themselves. They call for their calves and do not turn back. The test is answered plainly, and the Philistines can only go home.

The verb to return runs through the chapter, used of the ark's return again and again. In the next chapter the same verb will be used of Israel returning to the LORD.
passages.later: The book of Joshua lists Beth-shemesh among the towns given to the Levites: ‘Ain, Juttah, and Beth-shemesh’ (Joshua 21:16).
passages.asks: The cows walked away from their own calves, lowing as they went, because God was driving them. Ask where God has led you on a road you would not have chosen. And ask whether you are as quick to look up from your work and rejoice when something of God comes home.

passages.t: Who can stand before this holy God?
passages.happening:
The joy does not last. “But God struck down some of the people of Beth-shemesh because they looked inside the ark of the LORD. He struck down seventy men, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck them with a great slaughter” (verse 19).

The men of Beth-shemesh ask, “Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God? To whom should the ark go up from here?” (verse 20).

They send messengers to the people of Kiriath-jearim: “The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up with you” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The number in verse 19 has a history. Most Hebrew manuscripts read seventy men, fifty thousand men, a strange phrase that many scholars think was added by a copyist, since Beth-shemesh was a small town. Several manuscripts and translations, the Berean Standard Bible among them, read seventy. The ancient Greek translation words the first part of the verse differently and gives a different reason why the men were struck.

The chapter's end echoes the one before in reverse. The Philistines asked what to do with the ark and sent it away. Now the men of Beth-shemesh ask a deeper question, who can stand before this holy God, and they send it away too.

Kiriath-jearim lay higher in the hills to the northeast, on the road toward Jerusalem. The ark will stay there for twenty years, until David brings it to Jerusalem. The loss of Shiloh shaped Israel's life for a long time.
passages.later:
The law had warned that even the Levites who carried the holy things were not to look at them: they ‘are not to go in and look at the holy objects, even for a moment, or they will die’ (Numbers 4:20). Years later, when David brings the ark up to Jerusalem, a man named Uzzah dies beside it: ‘God struck him down on the spot for his irreverence’ (2 Samuel 6:7).

The question of verse 20 is asked again in the psalms: “Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? Who may stand in His holy place?” (Psalm 24:3).
passages.hard:
Why did God strike down the men of Beth-shemesh, who were Israelites glad that the ark had come home?

The judgment feels out of proportion. People who welcomed the ark with joy and sacrifice die for looking into it. The text's own explanation is that they looked inside the ark, treating the holiest object in Israel as something to inspect. The law had set strict limits around it. Beth-shemesh was a Levites' town, so its people had less excuse than the Philistines.

Some scholars prefer the ancient Greek text, which gives a different reason, that some did not rejoice, and think the Hebrew has suffered in copying. Others read the story as a sober lesson that God's presence is not safe to handle carelessly, even for his own people, as the story of Uzzah will show again. On any reading, the chapter wants readers to feel the danger as well as the joy of God's nearness.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The men of Beth-shemesh asked the right question, who can stand before this holy God, and then sent God away. Ask how you answer that question. And ask whether your nearness to holy things has made you careless with them.
